name: Agreement with the Iowa of May 20, 1890, ratified by the Act of February 13, 1891
aka: Jerome Commission (Cherokee Commission) agreement with the Iowa
citation: Act of February 13, 1891, ch. 165, 26 Stat. 749 (Iowa agreement at 753-758)
promises: Each member of the tribe could select an 80-acre allotment on the reservation set apart by the Executive Order of August 15, 1883 (Article II).
The allotments would be held in trust by the United States for 25 years, any conveyance of them in that time would be void, and were exempt from taxation and seizure (Article IV).
When the allotments were made, the United States would spend $24,000 for the Iowa on houses, breeding animals, farm implements and seeds (Article VI).
The United States would pay annuities for 25 years, starting at $3,600 a year for the first five years and falling to $1,200 a year for the last five (Article VII).
Nothing in the agreement would affect any other claim the Iowa had against the United States (Article VIII).

breaches.what: Under a special jurisdictional act, the Court of Claims found that the Jerome Commission orally promised the Iowa they would get as much for their surplus land as neighbouring tribes were later paid, that this promise was left out of the written agreement, and that the Sac and Fox and Kickapoo were paid $1.25 an acre against the Iowa's average of 38 cents. It awarded the tribe $254,632.59.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Court of Claims, Iowa Tribe of Indians v. United States, 68 Ct. Cl. 585 (No. 34677; decided May 6, 1929, new judgment December 2, 1929)

source.title: Iowa Tribe of Indians v. United States, 68 Ct. Cl. 585 (1929)
source.publisher: Caselaw Access Project, Harvard Law School

breaches.quote: clearly establishes the existence of an agreement, the terms of which are not expressed in the written contract

landTaken: The Court of Claims says 219,803 acres of surplus land were obtained at the 38-cent average, and that a later accurate survey found 50,818 acres more, which the Government sold to settlers at $1.25 an acre (68 Ct. Cl. 585).
compensation: Under the agreement: 80-acre allotments, $24,000 for improvements and 25 years of falling annuities, an average of 38 cents an acre for the surplus (Court of Claims). Awarded in 1929: $254,632.59 (68 Ct. Cl. 585). Whether and when it was paid was not confirmed.
today: In 1952 the Indian Claims Commission noted that the Iowa Tribe of the Iowa Reservation in Oklahoma, in Docket 79, was seeking an accounting arising from the Jerome Agreement of May 20, 1890; no Commission finding on that claim was located.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe's history page says its original Oklahoma reservation was established by executive order of August 15, 1883, and lists the President's message transmitting the 1890 Cherokee Commission agreement among its treaty documents.

openQuestions: Royce has no row for this cession (his Feb. 13, 1891 entry under 26 Stat. 749 is the Sauk and Fox only, pp. 938 and 940). The record uses area 649 because Article I cedes the reservation by the boundary Royce gives for 649; the allotted land stayed with the Iowa, so the drawn area is larger than what passed.

The court quotes House Report No. 581, 66th Congress, 2d session, which says an injustice was done to the Iowa of Oklahoma. That report was not opened, so it is not recorded as a government admission.
Whether the $254,632.59 judgment was paid, and how much went to attorneys (the act capped fees at 10 per cent), was not confirmed.

The 1929 opinion is the Court of Claims; no appeal to the Supreme Court was found. ICC full text searched (iowa 1890; iowa jerome): the only Iowa hit on the Jerome Agreement is the 1952 Docket 79 motion opinion, which does not decide it.

Audit 2026-11-10: 68 Ct. Cl. 585 opened on the Caselaw Access Project and confirmed (oral promise, 38 cents against $1.25, 219,803 and 50,818 acres, quote exact, judgment $254,632.59, new judgment Dec. 2, 1929). The court states the award but not how it was reached; its two figures, $193,253.00 and $63,597.00, sum to $256,850.00, so the award is not their sum. Plain lines reworded: promised now says surplus land, as the breach does; happened no longer says the commissioners paid the Iowa.

plain.promised: The Iowa gave up the surplus land of their Oklahoma reservation for 80-acre allotments each, $24,000 for homes and farming, and 25 years of annuities.
plain.happened: In 1929 the Court of Claims found US commissioners had orally promised the Iowa the same price neighbouring tribes got and left it out of the written deal. The neighbours got $1.25 an acre; the Iowa averaged 38 cents.
plain.today: The court awarded the tribe $254,632.59 in 1929. Whether it was paid is not confirmed.
